concepts.title: Why Local Government: Democracy at the Doorstep
concepts.definition: Local needs -- water, sanitation, street lights, schools -- are best judged where people live, so democratic theory reserves a tier of government for them. Local bodies bring government within reach: citizens can meet their representatives daily, and problems of the neighbourhood get institutions of their own.
concepts.key_idea: The problems closest to home need governments closest to home -- democracy scales down as well as up.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps208.txt lines 15-110 (introduction, why local governments, gandhi's gram swaraj idea, local needs and participation)
question_patterns: why do democracies need local self government

solution_steps.explain: Water supply, sanitation and local roads affect one locality, so decisions about them belong to that locality's elected body.
Small units let ordinary citizens contest, vote knowledgeably and watch results face to face.
Local bodies are schools of citizenship, breeding future leaders and habits of self-government.

concepts.title: 73rd and 74th Amendments: Constitutional Status to Local Bodies
concepts.definition: Before 1992 local bodies lived at the mercy of state governments, frequently superseded. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) changed that: panchayats and municipalities became constitutional institutions with regular five-year elections, reserved seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women, and State Election Commissions to conduct their polls.
concepts.key_idea: From favours to rights -- the 1992 amendments made local elections mandatory, not optional.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps208.txt lines 110-240 (73rd amendment and panchayati raj, 74th amendment and municipalities, five year term, reservations, state election commission)
question_patterns: what changes did the 73rd and 74th amendments bring

solution_steps.explain: Part IX (panchayats) and Part IXA (municipalities) made three-tier rural and urban local government a constitutional requirement.
Elections every five years, independent State Election Commissions, and fresh polls within six months of dissolution are mandatory.
Seats and chairperson posts are reserved for SCs, STs and -- one-third -- women, remaking who rules locally.

concepts.title: Panchayati Raj: The Three-Tier Rural Structure
concepts.definition: Rural local government now runs in three tiers -- gram panchayat at village level, panchayat samiti or block level, and zilla parishad at district level -- with the gram sabha of all voters above each panchayat. The eleventh schedule lists 29 subjects, from agriculture to rural housing, that state legislatures may devolve.
concepts.key_idea: Village to block to district -- three rungs of elected rural self-rule, capped by the assembly of all voters.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps208.txt lines 240-360 (three tier structure, gram panchayat gram sabha panchayat samiti zilla parishad, eleventh schedule subjects, functions and finances)
question_patterns: describe the three tier structure of panchayati raj
in class 11 local governments chapter: what is the gram sabha and why is it important

solution_steps.explain: Village gram panchayats, block panchayat samitis, and district zilla parishads form the ladder, with direct election at the base.
Every adult voter of the village area sits in the gram sabha, which approves plans and audits the panchayat's work.
The eleventh schedule's 29 subjects become real powers only when each state legislature passes them down with funds and functionaries.

concepts.title: Urban Local Government and Women's Leadership
concepts.definition: The 74th Amendment mapped urban areas to municipal corporations, municipal councils and nagar panchayats by size, with ward committees below. Reservation for women -- a third of seats and chairposts -- produced over a million elected women in local bodies, the world's largest cohort of women in public office, gradually shifting gender expectations of leadership.
concepts.key_idea: Cities get their own elected governments; women get seats by law -- and leadership follows the seat.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps208.txt lines 360-480 (municipal corporations councils nagar panchayats, ward committees, women's reservation and sarpanch pati phenomenon, significance of women in local politics)
question_patterns: which types of urban local bodies exist after the 74th amendment

solution_steps.explain: Big cities get municipal corporations, towns municipal councils, and transitional areas nagar panchayats, all directly elected by wards.
One-third of seats and chairperson positions are reserved for women, rotated among constituencies.
Beyond the early proxy-husband problem, evidence shows women representatives investing in water and services and normalising women's authority in public life.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Before 1992 a state government routinely suspended panchayats for years and ruled through its own nominees. Explain which changes after the 73rd Amendment prevent this.

solution_template.explain: Panchayats now enjoy a fixed five-year term, and any dissolution must be followed by fresh elections within six months.
The State Election Commission, insulated from the government, conducts and schedules these polls.
Suspension can no longer be a governing tool -- the amendment converted survival of panchayats into a constitutional right of local voters.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A newly elected woman sarpanch finds her husband signing papers and answering meetings in her name. What does this reveal, and how do the amendment's design and experience address it?

solution_template.explain: This is the sarpanch pati problem -- proxy rule by male relatives of women who hold reserved seats.
Direct election of the woman to the seat, gram sabha oversight, and rotation of reserved seats limit how long proxy rule can last.
Over terms, many women representatives overcome proxies and govern actively -- reservation builds leadership even if its first years are uneven.
